The Green tiger prawn Penaeus semisulcatus is a commercially important penaeid distributed across the Indo-West Pacific region, where it supports substantial trawl fisheries. Early life stages are planktonic, with newly hatched nauplii transitioning through several zoeal and mysis stages before metamorphosis. At the moment of hatching, each fertilised ovum yields a larva with an initial wet weight at birth of approximately 0.000274 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000274 grams], a value comparable to those reported for other caridean shrimp species with similar larval developmental modes. This minuscule starting mass necessitates rapid feeding on phytoplankton and microzooplankton during the early larval phase. The species exhibits notable sexual dimorphism in adult body size. For adult females, the ultimate abdominal length, measured from the base of the telson to the posterior margin of the carapace, reaches 5.5 centimetres [Li = 5.5 centimetres]. In contrast, adult males attain a smaller maximum body size, reflecting a common pattern among penaeid shrimp. Total length in this species can approach 23 centimetres from rostrum tip to telson apex, as documented in field surveys across its range.

Onset of sexual maturation in Penaeus semisulcatus is marked by a distinct shift in allometric growth, particularly in the carapace region. Females reach puberty at a carapace length of 3.22 centimetres [Lp = 3.22 centimetres], a morphological threshold that corresponds to the initiation of vitellogenesis and ovarian development. At this stage, the wet weight at puberty is approximately 26 grams [Wwp = approximately 26 grams], a value derived from the power relationship between body length and mass typical of penaeid crustaceans. This weight represents a substantial increase from the neonatal mass, underscoring the rapid growth achieved during the post-larval and juvenile phases. The physiological transition at puberty is accompanied by changes in hepatopancreatic function, as resources are increasingly allocated toward gonad maturation. In wild populations, variability in the timing of this transition is influenced by prevailing environmental conditions, with faster growth and earlier maturation observed in warmer, more productive coastal habitats. The abdominal muscle mass also increases markedly during this period, reflecting the energetic demands of both locomotion and reproductive preparation.

Reproductive output in female Green tiger prawns is tightly linked to body size and thermal regime. At a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) averaged approximately 14% [GSI = approximately 14%]. This index is comparable to values documented for the congeneric species Haliporoides sibogae, suggesting a conserved pattern of relative investment in gamete production among penaeids. The spawning season extends over several months in tropical waters, with individual females capable of multiple spawnings within a single reproductive cycle. Ovarian maturation proceeds through a series of distinct histological stages, from oogonial proliferation through primary and secondary vitellogenesis. Broodstock management in aquaculture operations routinely maintains water temperatures near this level to maximise egg production.

Adult body size in Penaeus semisulcatus exhibits a clear upper bound, with the ultimate wet weight for females recorded at 130 grams [Wwi = 130 grams] under favourable growing conditions. This asymptotic mass represents the maximum somatic investment achievable by the species, constrained by both metabolic limits and the physical capacity of the exoskeleton. Males typically attain a lower ultimate mass, rarely exceeding 80 to 90 grams in wild-caught specimens. The growth trajectory to this maximum size follows a sigmoidal pattern, with an initial rapid phase during the juvenile and sub-adult stages followed by a gradual plateau as the animal approaches its physiological ceiling. Factors such as food availability, stocking density in aquaculture settings, and water temperature interact to modulate the final body mass. In natural populations, the 130-gram upper mass is most frequently observed in older females inhabiting productive estuarine and coastal shelf environments where prey resources are abundant throughout the year. This size threshold also influences market value in commercial fisheries, with larger individuals commanding premium prices.

Longevity in Penaeus semisulcatus is relatively short compared to many marine decapods, reflecting a fast-paced life history characteristic of tropical penaeids. At a sustained water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 620 days [am = approximately 620 days], corresponding to roughly 1.7 years. This abbreviated lifespan is associated with rapid maturation, high fecundity, and substantial investment in a single, relatively brief reproductive window. Age determination in this species relies on modal progression analysis of carapace length-frequency data, as conventional hard-part ageing is not feasible due to the complete loss of calcified structures during each moult. The 620-day value is derived from field mark-recapture studies conducted in tropical Australian waters, where the species experiences year-round warm conditions. In contrast, populations at the cooler edge of the species range, such as those in the Mediterranean Sea where Penaeus semisulcatus has been introduced, may exhibit slightly extended longevity but reduced growth rates. The combination of rapidly attained adult body mass, early puberty, and high reproductive output within this compressed lifespan underscores the opportunistic, colonising life history strategy of this commercially vital penaeid.
